title: Make composition choices
summary: Choose emphasis and inspect the frame.
outcomes: Compare two choices and explain the result instead of applying a universal style rule.
startingAssumptions: No camera or external service is required; all measurements and scenes here are fictional.
editorialRationale: Original two-beat unrelated course fixture proving content-driven teaching and stable identities.

concepts.definition: Two or more visual elements attract attention in ways that may support or undermine the intended subject.
concepts.example: A different viewpoint removes the sign while keeping the expression and useful café context.

concepts.definition: The crop determines which surrounding information is included in the photograph.
concepts.example: More surroundings are included because they contribute to the intended story.

questions.prompt: The café sign competes with the face. Which comparison directly tests that distraction?

options.text: Keep the expression similar and change viewpoint to exclude the bright sign.
options.rationale: This tests the background distraction while preserving the intended subject.

options.text: Move the face onto a grid line while leaving the sign unchanged.
options.rationale: Grid alignment does not directly remove the competing contrast.

questions.prompt: Why might a wider café portrait be preferable to a tighter one?

options.text: The surroundings may be needed for the intended story.
options.rationale: A wider frame can preserve useful context when that is the objective.

options.text: A wider frame always creates a better photograph.
options.rationale: The choice depends on intent and what the added elements contribute.

beats.title: Give the viewer a first place to look
beats.outcome: Make a reasoned choice and identify what evidence would change it.
beats.explanation: A bright café sign can create [[photo-m02-attention-concept|competing emphasis]] beside a face. A centered portrait can be effective; moving the person onto a grid does not automatically solve a distracting background. Compare what the viewer notices before explaining your intention.

samajh.text: Do log ek saath zor se bolen to kiski baat sunoge?
samajh.mapping: Strong contrast can compete for attention, like two loud speakers.
samajh.boundary: Pictures are interpreted differently by different viewers; there is no guaranteed attention formula.

beats.hint: Return to the conditions stated in the comparison.

handbook.markdown: Ask a viewer what they notice first without coaching them. Their response is evidence about this frame, not a universal rule that every viewer will agree.

beats.recap: Two or more visual elements attract attention in ways that may support or undermine the intended subject.
beats.changeNote: This teaching beat is separate from earlier lesson completion.

beats.title: Treat the frame edges as decisions
beats.outcome: Make a reasoned choice and identify what evidence would change it.
beats.explanation: A [[photo-m02-edges-concept|context boundary]] can simplify a portrait or remove something needed to understand it. Inspect all four edges. A partial bright object may distract, but removing every surrounding detail can also erase the café story.

samajh.text: Kahani batate waqt kya andar rakhna hai, kya chhodna hai?
samajh.mapping: The frame is a boundary around selected information.
samajh.boundary: A crop cannot explain all context, and omitted details may change interpretation.

beats.hint: Return to the conditions stated in the comparison.

handbook.markdown: Compare a tight and wide crop and name exactly what meaning was gained or lost. Then check bright intrusions and awkward cutoffs separately.

beats.recap: The crop determines which surrounding information is included in the photograph.

recap.title: Make composition choices: recap
recap.markdown: State the intention, compare a meaningful alternative, then inspect the result. Separate observed differences from your interpretation.

appliedTask.title: Explain two versions of the scene
appliedTask.prompt: Propose two portrait frames that balance the person and café context.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Compare a tighter frame that emphasizes expression with a wider frame that includes the café deliberately. Inspect the bright menu at the edge; either include it as useful context or change viewpoint so it stops competing. Explain why the chosen version better fits the story.
appliedTask.reasoning: A defensible answer relates the decision to an intention and names a way to compare it.
